current.query: CPR 31.6 standard disclosure documents party relies on adverse documents support another party's case
current.answer:
Standard disclosure is the disclosure order under CPR Part 31 where a party must disclose only the documents on which it relies, the documents that adversely affect its own case or another party’s case, the documents that support another party’s case, and any documents required by a relevant practice direction. [4]

To give standard disclosure, the party must make a reasonable search for those documents, and the reasonableness of the search depends on factors such as the number of documents, the nature and complexity of the case, the ease and expense of retrieval, and the significance of any likely documents. [5]

After the search, the party must make a list of the documents it knows about that fall within rule 31.6 and that are or have been in its control, unless rule 31.10(8) applies. [9]

PD 31A says the list should be in Form N265. [11]

If you want, I can also give the rule for standard disclosure in the Commercial Court where PD 57AD does not apply.

results.name: Summary Judgment
results.question: How do I apply for summary judgment?

current.query: CPR Part 24 summary judgment application no real prospect of succeeding no other compelling reason for a trial
current.answer:
Under CPR Part 24, summary judgment is a procedure by which the court may decide a claim or issue without a trial. [1]

The court may give summary judgment if a party has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim, defence or issue, and there is no other compelling reason for a trial. [3]

A claimant may not apply until the defendant has filed an acknowledgment of service or a defence, unless the court gives permission or another rule or practice direction says otherwise. [4]

Where a summary judgment hearing is fixed, the respondent must be given at least 14 days’ notice of the hearing date and the issues the court is asked to decide. [4]

If you want, I can also give the court-specific practice for a particular court, such as the Chancery Division.

results.question: What are the time limits for filing an appeal?

current.query: CPR Part 52 appeal time limit filing appellant's notice permission to appeal notice of appeal 21 days
current.answer:
Generally, you must file an appellant’s notice within the time limit directed by the lower court, or if no direction has been given, within 21 days of the date of the decision being appealed. [1]

Time runs from the date the decision is pronounced in court or the judgment is handed down, even if the written order is produced later. [1]

There are also specific shorter time limits in some cases, and the shortest time limit is 7 days from the date of the decision being appealed. [2]

For appeals under CPR Part 52, the rules apply to appeals to the Court of Appeal, High Court and County Court, and there are special provisions for some categories of appeal. [7]

If you want the exact deadline for a particular kind of appeal, tell me which court or type of decision it is, because the sources show different time limits in different cases. [2][9]

current.answer:
The material retrieved is **court-specific**, from the Senior Courts Costs Office Guide, so it does not by itself establish the general CPR position. [2]

In that guide, “costs” normally fall into two categories: disbursements such as counsel’s fees, court fees and witness expenses, and the fees legal representatives charge their client, sometimes called “profit costs”. [2]

The guide also says costs payable by one party to another can, in appropriate circumstances, include costs incurred before proceedings were issued. [2]

As to who pays, the guide says no party has a right to costs and costs are in the court’s discretion, but the general rule is that the unsuccessful party will be ordered to pay the successful party’s costs. [5]

The guide also says the court can make an order reflecting the extent to which each party has been successful on different issues. [5]

For litigants in person, the guide says recoverable costs can include out-of-pocket expenses, payments for expert assistance in assessing the claim for costs, costs for work that caused pecuniary loss, and costs for work that did not cause pecuniary loss. [1]

In the TCC guide, costs disputes are resolved under CPR Part 44, and interlocutory hearings of one day or less will usually be subject to summary assessment of costs. [3]

The available sources do not directly give the general CPR rules on costs; you may want to check the CPR/Practice Direction source or refine the query to a specific topic such as entitlement, summary assessment, detailed assessment, or costs budgeting.

current.query: CPR Part 6 service of claim form methods of service deemed service time for service
current.answer:
Under CPR Part 6, a claim form may be served by personal service, first class post/document exchange/other next-business-day delivery, leaving it at a permitted address, fax or other electronic communication, or a court-authorised method. [3]

The court will serve the claim form unless a rule or practice direction says the claimant must serve it, the claimant says they want to serve it, or the court orders otherwise. [4]

Part 6 applies to service of documents generally, but other Parts or practice directions can make different provision for particular claims. [1]

If you want, I can also give the rule on where the claim form must be served or the time limit for service.
